script.opening: “I’m ringing about my mum, Iris Paterson, at Beech House. She’s been scratching herself raw for weeks and nobody’s done anything. Now my own hands are itching. What is going on? Is she being neglected?”

facts.text: Helen, daughter, holds a registered health and welfare LPA for Iris. Visits twice a week. Calling from work at lunchtime.

About six weeks. Worse at night; staff say she is restless and scratching. Yesterday Helen saw red spots and scratch marks on her wrists, between her fingers, round her waist and under her breasts. The skin on her hands is thick, grey and crusty, “like dried porridge”. Not on her face. Eating and drinking as usual; no fever; no new confusion beyond her usual.
Emollient and hydrocortisone cream from four weeks ago, applied by staff. No better. Nobody from the practice has seen her skin.
Helen’s hands and wrists itch at night for a week; her husband not yet. A carer mentioned two staff members and the resident next door are itching too. Helen does not know names.
Alzheimer’s for five years, cannot make decisions about treatment now. Donepezil, amlodipine. No steroid tablets or immunosuppressants. Mobile with a frame.
Feels the home ignored it and the practice “just sent a cream”. Wants to know who else is affected and whether she should report the home.

Angry and upset at first. Calms if the doctor takes her seriously, explains what it probably is and gives a clear plan for today. Pushes for names of other residents; accepts the confidentiality explanation if it is given respectfully. Relieved to hear she can be involved in decisions.

ice.ideas: “Something catching that the home has let spread, and nobody looked properly.”
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA: guilt that she did not push sooner, and fear that she has carried it home to her grandchildren. Also worried her mother is being neglected.
ice.expectations: “Someone to see Mum today, tell me what it is, and tell me who else has it.”

cues: Itch worse at night in the hands, wrists and waist, plus others itching — classic pattern of scabies in a closed setting.
Thick, crusty skin on the hands — possible crusted scabies, highly infectious.
“Is she being neglected?” — respond honestly, without defensiveness.
“Who else has it?” — confidentiality of other residents.

checkpoints.text: Takes a focused third-party history: distribution, nocturnal itch, duration, treatment so far, others affected (staff, residents, family), crusting, systemic features and medicines
Recognises a probable scabies outbreak in a care home, with possible crusted scabies in Iris, and considers other causes of itch in older people
Arranges same-day face-to-face assessment at the home, and does not rely on further remote prescribing

Explains that the care home should inform the UKHSA health protection team, who coordinate outbreak management: simultaneous treatment of all residents, staff and close contacts, environmental measures, and specialist advice on oral ivermectin for crusted scabies (check the SPC/local formulary)
Advises Helen to treat herself and her household at the same time as the home (permethrin cream, two applications 7 days apart, via pharmacy or her own GP), with washing of clothes and bedding
Involves Helen as Iris’s health and welfare attorney in best-interests decisions about treatment, and explains that Iris lacks capacity for this decision
Keeps other residents’ information confidential and explains why respectfully

Responds to the neglect question honestly: acknowledges the earlier prescription without examination, explains how it will be reviewed, and signposts routes for concerns (home manager, practice complaints, CQC; safeguarding if indicators)

worked.txt: “Thank you for ringing, and I’m sorry your mum’s been so uncomfortable. Let me ask a few questions so I can work out what’s going on today.”

“An itch that’s worse at night, in the hands, wrists and waist, with staff and you itching too, sounds very much like scabies, tiny mites that spread through close skin contact. The thick crusty skin on her hands makes me think she may have a heavier form, which spreads more easily.”

“I’d like a doctor to see her at the home today, rather than another cream over the phone. If it’s scabies, the home needs to contact the public health team, who organise treating everyone at the same time.”
“As her attorney for health decisions, you’ll be involved in agreeing her treatment. Your mum isn’t able to decide this herself now, so we’ll decide together what’s in her best interests.”
“I can’t tell you about other residents, in the same way I wouldn’t share your mum’s details with their families. The public health team will make sure everyone affected is treated.”

“You’re right that a cream was prescribed without anyone looking at her skin, and that should have been different. I’ll make sure that’s reviewed. If you want to raise concerns formally, I can explain how.”

f.learning: Generalised itch in an older care-home resident needs examination and a broad differential (dry skin, drugs, eczema, systemic disease), but itch worse at night affecting the hands, wrists, waist and breasts, with staff, other residents and visitors itching, is scabies until proven otherwise. In older people with dementia or immunosuppression, scabies may be atypical or crusted (hyperkeratotic, Norwegian) scabies: thick, crusted scaling, often on the hands, with very large numbers of mites and high infectivity. Topical steroids alone can mask it and make it worse. UKHSA guidance on scabies in care homes and other closed settings advises that when scabies is suspected in a care home, the home should contact the local health protection team; outbreaks are managed by coordinated, simultaneous treatment of all residents, staff and close contacts (including families), environmental cleaning and laundering, and, in crusted scabies or outbreaks, consideration of oral ivermectin under specialist or UKHSA advice (check the SPC/local formulary). Topical permethrin 5% is applied to the whole body (including scalp, face and neck in older people, avoiding the eyes) and repeated after 7 days. Itch can persist for several weeks after successful treatment. For a resident who lacks capacity, treatment decisions are made in her best interests, involving a registered health and welfare attorney (Mental Capacity Act 2005). Other residents’ information is confidential. When a relative asks about neglect, respond honestly, acknowledge any shortcomings (such as prescribing without examination), and explain routes for concerns; a delayed diagnosis is not in itself neglect, but safeguarding should be considered if there are wider indicators.

knowledge.summary: A care-home resident with dementia has six weeks of nocturnal itch in a scabies distribution and crusted skin on her hands; staff, another resident and her daughter are itching. Treat as a probable scabies outbreak with possible crusted scabies: same-day examination, the home to contact the UKHSA health protection team, simultaneous treatment of residents, staff and contacts, Helen and her household treated at the same time, best-interests decisions with Helen as attorney, confidentiality for others, and an honest response about the earlier remote prescription.

points.t: Nocturnal itch; burrows and papules in finger webs, wrists, waist, breasts and genitals; itch in contacts. In older people the pattern can be atypical and the face and scalp involved [2].
Thick, crusted, scaly plaques, often on the hands, in older, immunosuppressed or cognitively impaired people. Very high mite load and infectivity; may itch little [1,2].

The care home should contact the UKHSA health protection team when scabies is suspected. Outbreak management includes case finding, simultaneous treatment of residents, staff and contacts, and environmental measures [1].
Permethrin 5% cream to the whole body, repeated after 7 days (check the SPC/local formulary). In crusted scabies or outbreaks, oral ivermectin may be advised by specialists or UKHSA [1,6].
Household and close contacts treated at the same time, even without symptoms. Wash clothing, towels and bedding at 50°C or above, or seal in bags for 72 hours [2].
Itch may last 2–4 weeks; persistent itch beyond that, new burrows or crusting suggests treatment failure or reinfestation.
If the resident lacks capacity for the decision, treat in her best interests and consult the registered health and welfare attorney [3].
Do not disclose other residents’ details [4]. Be open about shortcomings in care and explain how to raise concerns [5].

model.text: Hello, I’m Dr Clarke. Can I check who I’m speaking to and your connection to the patient?

Helen Paterson, I’m her daughter, I have power of attorney for health. I’m ringing about my mum, Iris, at Beech House. She’s been scratching herself raw for weeks and nobody’s done anything. Now my own hands are itching. Is she being neglected?

Thank you, Helen. I can see the health and welfare LPA on her record. I’m sorry she’s been so uncomfortable, and I’ll come back to your question about neglect. Can I ask some questions first so I can work out what’s going on?
Fine.
Where on her body is it, and is it worse at any time of day?
Wrists, between her fingers, round her waist, under her breasts. The staff say she’s worse at night. And her hands have gone thick and crusty, like dried porridge.
Is anyone else itching? You mentioned your hands.
My hands and wrists, at night, for a week. A carer said two staff are itching and the lady next door.
Is your mum otherwise herself? Any fever, more confused than usual, off her food? Any new medicines, or steroid tablets?
No, she’s the same as usual. No new tablets apart from the creams.

An itch that’s worse at night in the hands, wrists and waist, with staff and you itching too, sounds very much like scabies. That’s tiny mites that spread through close skin contact. It’s nothing to do with cleanliness. The thick crusty skin on her hands makes me think she may have a heavier form, called crusted scabies, which spreads more easily. A steroid cream can make scabies worse.
Scabies? In a care home?
It’s quite common in care homes, because of close contact during personal care. The important thing is to deal with it properly now.
What’s worrying you most?
That I didn’t push sooner. That I’ve taken it home to my grandchildren. And who else has it.

Here’s what will happen today. A doctor will see your mum at the home this afternoon, rather than another cream over the phone. If it’s scabies, the home needs to contact the public health team, who organise treating all the residents, staff and close contacts at the same time, and advise on cleaning. With crusted scabies they may also advise tablets as well as cream.
Because your mum can’t make this decision herself now, as her attorney you’ll be involved in agreeing her treatment, in her best interests. Is that okay?
Yes. Please.

For you and your household, including the grandchildren if they’ve had close contact: get permethrin cream from the pharmacy or your own GP, apply it all over, and repeat after a week, ideally starting on the same day as the home. Wash clothes, towels and bedding on a hot wash. The itch can last a few weeks even after it’s worked.
And the others at the home? Who are they?
I can’t share other residents’ details, in the same way I wouldn’t share your mum’s with their families. The public health team will make sure everyone affected is treated.

About neglect: you’re right that a cream was prescribed without anyone looking at her skin, and that should have been different. I’ll make sure it’s reviewed. If you want to raise concerns about the home or about us, I can explain how, including speaking to the home manager or the Care Quality Commission.
Can I check what you’ll do from here?
Doctor sees Mum today. Home calls public health. I get the cream for us, twice a week apart, hot wash. You’ll look at what went wrong.
Exactly. I’ll ring you after the visit. If your mum gets a fever, becomes more confused or drowsy, or the skin becomes hot, red and weeping, the home should call us or 111 urgently.

social.t: Visiting relatives are close contacts and may carry scabies to grandchildren. Coordinated treatment includes them.
Relatives of care-home residents often feel guilty about not noticing sooner. Acknowledge it.

legal.t: A registered attorney can make health decisions the person lacks capacity to make, in their best interests (Mental Capacity Act 2005).
Other residents’ health information cannot be shared with a relative without their consent or another lawful basis (GMC Confidentiality).

professional.t: Prescribing for a rash without examination, at a third party’s request, risks missed diagnoses. Review it as a significant event.
Be open when care has fallen short and explain how concerns can be raised.

community.t: Lead outbreak management in care homes, advising on treatment, staff, visitors and environmental measures.
Relatives can share concerns about a care home with the CQC; the home and the practice also have complaints processes.

pitfalls.intro: The diagnosis is in the pattern. The marks are in acting as an outbreak, involving the attorney properly, protecting others’ confidentiality and answering the neglect question honestly.

items.why: Scabies and crusted scabies need examination and coordinated treatment.

items.fail: Not asking who else is itching.
items.why: Itching contacts are the diagnostic clue and drive outbreak management.

Health protection team; simultaneous treatment of residents, staff and families.

items.why: Damages trust and misses a learning event.

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: The diagnosis is in the pattern. The marks are in acting as an outbreak, involving the attorney properly, protecting others’ confidentiality and answering the neglect question honestly.

items.fail: Prescribing another cream over the phone.
items.why: Scabies and crusted scabies need examination and coordinated treatment.

items.fail: Not asking who else is itching.
items.why: Itching contacts are the diagnostic clue and drive outbreak management.
items.fix: Ask about staff, residents and visitors.
Health protection team; simultaneous treatment of residents, staff and families.
Explain why you cannot, and how they will be treated.

items.fail: Ignoring or deflecting the neglect question.
items.why: Damages trust and misses a learning event.
items.fix: Acknowledge the remote prescription; explain how to raise concerns.

items.why: Iris lacks capacity; Helen has a health and welfare LPA.
